content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Consensus identifies the cedar primarily as a symbol of strength, majesty, and enduring stature applied especially to the flourishing of the righteous under God's blessing (Ps 92:12 as anchor), with common alternatives of (a) human pride/imperial power destined for judgment (Isa 2:13; Ezek 31), (b) messianic/Davidic kingdom planting (Ezek 17:22-24), and minority senses of purification (Lev 14; Num 19) and temple/divine dwelling. Consensus treats the positive and negative uses as distinct senses, with the positive one primary.","book_summary":"The book identifies the cedar as one single symbol: towering stature — 'a power of great height and majesty, whoever bears it.' Assyria, the house of David, and the righteous are all instances of the same symbol; the symbol denotes the stature itself, deliberately neutral as to the bearer's identity or moral standing.","consensus_core_identification":"Cedar = strength/majesty/enduring stature, primarily as an image of the righteous person's God-blessed flourishing, with pride-ripe-for-judgment as a distinct secondary sense.","book_core_identification":"Cedar = great height/majesty/power as such, a valence-neutral image of towering stature applicable to any bearer (Assyria, Davidic house, the righteous); the moral coloring belongs to the context, not the symbol.","core_relation":"BOOK_BROADENS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The consensus partitions cedar usage into a primary positive sense (righteous flourishing) and a separate negative sense (pride judged); the book collapses these into one neutral symbol of towering power. The book thus removes the positive-valence restriction from the primary meaning and reclassifies the pride/judgment and messianic uses from alternative meanings into ordinary instances of the single core symbol ('the stature, not the nation's identity'). It also silently drops the purification/temple-material senses the consensus lists.","material_contradiction":"None. Both agree the cedar's semantic engine is height/majesty/strength; the disagreement is over whether the righteous-flourishing application is the primary meaning or merely one instantiation of a neutral stature symbol.","rationale":"The book preserves the consensus's central referent — the cedar as an image of majestic, towering stature — so the cores are not contradictory. But it materially changes precision and boundaries: where the consensus privileges the positive 'flourishing righteous' sense and treats pride/judgment and messianic planting as separate senses, the book unifies all uses under one valence-neutral definition ('whoever bears it'), making moral evaluation contextual rather than part of the symbol. This is a genuine boundary reclassification within the same category, fitting REFINED with BOOK_BROADENS at the core and PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION in extension. Several consensus responses (C, D, and A's notes) already gesture toward this bivalence, but none states the neutral unification as the core identification.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue MATCH: the consensus responses themselves acknowledge cedar as a bivalent symbol whose common denominator is height/majesty, and Response C's primary meaning ('strength, majesty, lofty stature... in positive contexts the righteous or divinely established rule') comes very close to the book's neutral-stature formulation, making the book's move arguably just a cleaner wording of what the consensus already says rather than a material boundary change.","confidence":"medium"}
